newsitem.title: ROMANIA: ROMANIA TO START CREDIT TALKS WITH THE IMF.
newsitem.headline: ROMANIA TO START CREDIT TALKS WITH THE IMF.

text.p: International Monetary Fund negotiatior, Poul Thomsen, will arrive in Bucharest on Tuesday to start talks with the country's ruling coalition on resuming Fund credits suspended last year.
"Thomsen is due in Bucharest later today. His team of experts are already here and loan talks are expected to start on Wednesday," a central bank official told Reuters.
Negotiations with the IMF, expected to take up to three weeks, coincide with ongoning loan talks with the World Bank and the European Union.

The Fund agreed to abandon a previous $460 million three-year standby accord -- halted due to foreign exchange market restrictions and overspending by the former leftist government -- and to begin talks on a new arrangement.
An IMF mission last December judged that Romania had sunk into an economic crisis grimmer than it had been thought it was when ex-communists were defeated in elections last November.
Latest data show year-on-year inflation was 56.9 percent in 1996, almost three times targetted 20 percent.
The 1996 budget deficit soared to 5.7 percent of gross domestic product from initial pledges of 2.2 percent, while the current account deficit is expected to hit $2.0 billion.
The new cabinet is now working on a package to restore macro-economic stability and step up reforms.
Its governing programme, though lacking figures, pledges to tackle economic imbalances, accelerate structural reforms and boost social benefits.

Cutting budget spending, maintain free exchange markets and restructure energy-intensive and farming sectors are the key elements which would help the Balkan country to win Fund approval for renewed credits.

Last week, Romania's central bank governor Mugur Isarescu urged quick reform of the economy to underpin tightened monetary policies coupled with a planned liberalisation of the local foreign exchange market.

The BNR has already started to tighten policies, lifting its key rates to restore confidence in the sagging leu currency, which plunged by about 30 percent to 5,450/500 against the dollar since January 1.
